dmbok_terms: separation of duty between oversight and execution
Data Governance Council (final review and adoption)
positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 keeps governance as oversight separate from execution and gives approval to defined roles, so that a Data Owner holds approval authority over decisions about data in a domain and, once stewards and management have refined a draft, the Data Governance Council (or similar body) makes the final review and adoption. It names decision rights as a governance issue type and expects the strategy to define an operating framework that settles who governs; it says nothing about AI agents, so the AI-may versus human-approves split is project-specific.
rationales: Compared README.md (principle: AI proposes, evidence supports, the Data Steward evaluates, the appropriate human owner approves; 'Human accountability remains explicit') and the HANDOFF.md decision model (the 'AI may' list and the 'Human approval required' list). The principle matches the DMBOK2 pattern of drafting, steward review and owner or council approval, with oversight kept apart from execution. Rated Partial because the approving party is only 'the appropriate human owner', whereas the DMBOK2 expects accountabilities and the identity of the governing body to be explicit; naming a holder is handled under A-04. Suggested wording: define 'the appropriate human owner' in DMBOK2 role terms (Data Owner for decisions on data within a domain; the governing council or its delegate for policy and standards), labelled general industry context and subject to human approval.
caveats: Chapter 3 does not mention AI or automated agents, so the list of what AI may do has no DMBOK2 passage behind it.

The DMBOK2 text gives no decision-rights matrix; the Data Owner and council roles are described in general terms, and the sample policies in section 2.7 are illustrations of possible policy shapes, not requirements.

dmbok_terms: types of Data Stewards (Business, Enterprise, Technical, Coordinating, Executive, Chief)
positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 defines stewardship as accountability and responsibility for the processes that ensure effective control and use of data assets, with steward work typically covering core Metadata and the business glossary, documented rules and standards, identifying and resolving data quality issues (or facilitating their resolution) and day-to-day adherence to governance policies, and it lets stewards be differentiated by organisational place and focus, for example Business or Enterprise Data Stewards. It presents governance-level issue management as relieving production support teams, which implies governance work is distinct from production support without taking issue resolution out of steward scope.

Chapter 16 treats the Data Steward as a business role centred on data governance: a recognised subject matter expert accountable for metadata and data quality of business entities, subject areas or databases, who typically defines business terms, quality requirements and business rules and helps identify and resolve data issues, with emphasis varying by organisation. It assigns handling of information-system problems to a separate IT help-desk role and shows fitness-for-use monitoring and root-cause contribution under a hybrid Data Quality Analyst role.
rationales: Compared README.md (the target role is 'a data governance role rather than an operational incident-resolution role', with a responsibility list running from data quality and business definitions through lineage, governance reporting and continuous improvement) and the HANDOFF.md non-goal of resolving operational incidents on behalf of operations teams. The list covers most DMBOK2 steward focus areas, but the row is Partial because (1) the role is not mapped to any DMBOK2 steward type; (2) the DMBOK2 counts identifying and resolving data issues, or facilitating resolution, as steward work, so the exclusion should be worded as excluding production-support incident handling and not data issue management (not rated Divergent because the DMBOK2 itself separates governance issue management from production support); (3) business rules, data standards and policy adherence are not named in the README list, which is a point to confirm because the DMBOK2 says steward focus varies. Adopting any option is a human decision and internal role definitions outrank the DMBOK2.

Compared README.md (Business context: the scope list and the statement that the role is 'a data governance role rather than an operational incident-resolution role') and HANDOFF.md (non-goal: resolving operational incidents on behalf of operations teams). The governance framing and the scope (quality, definitions, critical data elements, dictionaries, documentation, rules and controls, root cause) match the Chapter 16 steward and hybrid role descriptions, and keeping incident handling out of the role matches Chapter 16's separate IT issue-handling role. The only friction is vocabulary: the DMBOK2 says stewards help identify and resolve data issues, so a short clarifying phrase avoids an apparent conflict. Suggested wording: 'a data governance role that analyses data issues and root causes and recommends action, rather than an operational incident-resolution role'.
caveats: The DMBOK2 steward types are given as examples and the book says steward focus differs between organisations, so the absence of a DMBOK2 activity from the README list is not necessarily a gap.
The DMBOK2 passages describe stewardship in organisations generally; none addresses stewards working with AI agents.
Reading limited to Chapters 15-16: steward types, the full catalogue of steward responsibilities and the Data Owner role sit in the data governance chapter, which this reader did not cover.
Linking 'operational incident-resolution' to the Help Desk Administrator role is this reader's analogy; the DMBOK2 does not say stewards exclude incident handling.

Mapping, lineage, data-contract and upstream-dependency duties resemble the IT and hybrid roles in 7.2.3 and 7.2.4; the DMBOK2 says stewards play different roles by organisational priority and does not forbid a broader scope.
proposal_options: Option 1 - Business Data Steward: adopt this DMBOK2 steward type as the label for the target role (business professionals, most often subject matter experts, accountable for a subset of data and working with stakeholders to define and control it) [DMBOK2-C03-23, DMBOK2-C03-24]. Fits a steward who works with SMEs and Data Owners on Investment Operations definitions and quality; implies business-side accountability for a data subset.

Option 2 - Enterprise Data Steward: adopt this type instead, because it describes oversight of a data domain across business functions [DMBOK2-C03-22]. Fits a steward who spans definitions, mappings, lineage and quality across the whole Investment Operations data domain; implies a wider remit than a single subset.

Option 3 - keep the neutral title 'Data Steward' and add only a one-line note that the DMBOK2 stewardship definition and focus areas are general industry context [DMBOK2-C03-14]; the DMBOK2 says stewards may be differentiated by place or focus and that terms such as custodian or trustee are used for steward-like functions, so no single label is required [DMBOK2-C03-20, DMBOK2-C03-15].

positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 defines a Data Owner as a business Data Steward with approval authority over decisions about data within a domain, has the operating model settle where accountability and ownership reside, records the steward responsible for each glossary term as term metadata, and lists conflicts over data ownership among governance issues. A sample policy in section 2.7 has business owners approved by the Data Governance Office, which illustrates owner designation as a governed approval.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: Chapter 10 says shared Reference and Master Data belong to the organisation rather than to one application or department, makes Business Data Stewards accountable for Reference Data quality, and counts finding out who is responsible for definition and maintenance as part of Reference Data Management because missing accountability is a risk. It suggests recording the steward's name as metadata for each Reference Data set, notes that change-approval workflows rely on knowing who is responsible, offers a steward-coverage metric for spotting gaps in support, and treats deciding who is accountable for which decisions as a governance and cultural question for stewards, architects, managers, executives and bodies such as the Data Governance Council.

Within Chapters 15-16 the DMBOK2 names ownership and accountability as basic questions an organisation must clarify, warns that data ownership is hard to define under a decentralised model, lists owners alongside stewards and custodians as frontline roles, and expects roles to be given to people at a suitable level. It does not, in this range, define the Data Owner role, say who approves an ownership assignment, or describe detecting ownership gaps.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md ('ownership assignment' under 'Human approval required'; acting as the Data Owner is a non-goal) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (ownership gaps are among the things the agent identifies; 'Assigning owners' is under not_responsible_for; 'Any ownership assignment' is under human_approval_required_for). Using 'Data Owner' for the approving human, requiring human approval for assignment and surfacing missing owners all match the DMBOK2. The project does not name the body that approves an assignment (the DMBOK2 sample names the Data Governance Office); that is carried under A-04. Suggested citation: reference the DMBOK2 Data Owner definition as general industry context where the project's roles are described.

Compared HANDOFF.md ('ownership assignment' under Human approval required; 'acts as the Data Owner' among the non-goals), ARCHITECTURE.md (Definition & CDE Agent: 'identify ownership gaps'; prohibited: 'assigning owners') and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (responsible_for 'ownership gaps'; not_responsible_for 'Assigning owners'; human_approval_required_for 'Any ownership assignment'; output field ownership_gaps typed as an array of strings). The decision rights agree in substance with Chapter 10, which also leaves accountability decisions to people and governance bodies and treats missing accountability as a risk to be detected. The status is Partial rather than Aligned because the repository uses 'Data Owner' and 'ownership gap' without defining either, names no field or measure for recording or checking who is responsible, and does not use Chapter 10's terms (steward accountability, steward name, steward coverage). Proposed wording change, for human approval: define 'ownership gap' once (a term, element or data set with no named accountable party), note its correspondence to the Chapter 10 steward-coverage gap as GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT, and keep 'Data Owner' as the internal term until the owner settles the role vocabulary, which belongs to chapters outside this unit.

Compared HANDOFF.md ('Human approval required' lists ownership assignment) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (the agent identifies 'ownership gaps' and is not responsible for 'Assigning owners'). Keeping assignment with humans and only surfacing gaps fits the DMBOK2 emphasis on clarifying ownership and accountability. However 'Data Owner' and 'appropriate human owner' are not defined or named anywhere in the repository, and Phase 0b of docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md plans to name only the governance sign-off and override roles, not Data Owners for data domains, so no named role is yet accountable for approving an assignment. Suggested wording: define 'Data Owner' and 'ownership gap' in the project's own terms, state which named role approves assignments once Phase 0b names it, and keep any DMBOK2 usage labelled general industry context; the structural choices for naming roles are set out under A-04.
caveats: The business-owner approval example is one of several illustrative policy shapes in section 2.7, not a requirement.

The DMBOK2 makes a Data Owner a type of business Data Steward, whereas the project separates the evaluating Data Steward from the approving Data Owner; the book lets stewards differ by place and focus, so this is a terminology note, not a conflict.
The range read does not use the phrase 'ownership gap'; linking it to a missing owner or missing responsible steward on a glossary term is an inference.

Chapter 10 does not define a 'Data Owner' role; it speaks of organisational ownership and accountable Business Data Stewards, so the Data Owner versus Data Steward vocabulary has to be settled from the governance and organisation chapters, which are outside this unit's range.

Watch point: because Chapter 10 places shared data with the organisation, naming a single department or application team as Data Owner of shared reference or master data would need to be reconciled with that principle; the files compared make no such assignment.

The label 'Data Steward coverage' sits at the end of PDF page 626 and the cited sentence continues on page 627. Table 23 (Critical Reference Data Metadata Attributes) is a missing figure, so whether it lists an owner or steward attribute is unverifiable from text; only the steward-name item in the section 2.2.5 text is relied on.

Chapters 15-16 contain no Data Owner definition and no guidance on ownership-gap detection or on who approves an ownership assignment; the main Data Owner treatment lies outside the assigned range and was not read.
The status therefore rests on general statements about ownership and accountability, not on a role definition to compare against.

positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 gives governance a judicial-like function of issue management and escalation, usually carried out through several committees of differing purpose and oversight, lets each organisation choose a model that fits its culture (including a virtual team with specific accountabilities), expects C-level sponsorship for a formal programme, and has the strategy define an operating framework with accountabilities. Its escalation path has stewardship teams resolve many issues locally, requires issues needing escalation to be logged and allows them to go up to the Data Governance Council, and sends issues the council cannot resolve to corporate governance or management.

The DMBOK2 expects governance work to be done by a Data Governance Steering Committee and working groups under any operating model, wants such leadership forums to be genuine decision-making bodies, and looks for an executive sponsor (ideally the CDO), while offering a single accountable leader or a RACI matrix as ways to make accountability explicit and noting that an operating model supplies a process for resolving issues. For a maturity assessment it adds that, absent formal governance, oversight falls to the steering committee or management layer that started the work.
rationales: Compared agents/factory/agent-risk-reviewer.md (only a 'named human governance owner' may approve; contested cut/redesign findings route to that owner with the override logged; the role is not yet named and escalations default to the project owner) and docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md Phase 0b (name the accountable human roles, including who holds override authority). A single accountable human escalation point is compatible with the DMBOK2's allowance for a virtual governance team, but the project defines no governance bodies or levels, no escalation path beyond the override log, and no named holder. Rated Partial: the principle of a named human owner is present, while defined accountabilities, bodies and a logged multi-step escalation path, which the DMBOK2 describes as parts of a working operating framework, are not yet. Adopting any option is a human decision and internal governance arrangements outrank the DMBOK2.

Compared agents/factory/agent-risk-reviewer.md (approval and contested-finding escalations go to a 'named human governance owner'; an assumption records that the role is unspecified and escalations route to the project owner until named) and docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md Phase 0b (name who holds Factory-tier sign-off, operational-tier sign-off and override authority). A human decision-maker and an escalation route match the DMBOK2 intent, but no governance forum, sponsor or accountability map exists yet, so the owner is a placeholder rather than a role within a stated governance structure. All three options below are proposals for the project owner; the DMBOK2 is general industry context and internal policy outranks it.
caveats: unverifiable from text: Table 4 (typical governance committees and bodies), Figure 16 (governance organization parts), Figure 19 (example operating framework) and Figure 20 (data issue escalation path) are images with dead links, so committee names, memberships and the exact escalation levels cannot be confirmed; the position rests on the surrounding prose only.
The DMBOK2 leaves the choice of governance model to each organisation; any body named in the options is a proposal for human decision, and internal governance arrangements outrank the DMBOK2.

The Chapter 15 fallback concerns oversight of a maturity assessment, so likening it to the project's 'defaults to the project owner' arrangement is an analogy, not DMBOK2 guidance on escalation paths.
The assigned chapters do not describe an escalation path in those terms; the nearest statement is that an operating model provides a process to resolve issues.
proposal_options: Option 1 - single accountable owner (virtual model): name one human governance owner and a deputy as the escalation and approval endpoint, optionally titled Chief Data Steward since the DMBOK2 lets such a steward chair governance bodies in lieu of a CDO [DMBOK2-C03-21], within a governance team that may be virtual with specific accountabilities [DMBOK2-C03-04]; record the role in a short operating framework and accountabilities statement [DMBOK2-C03-32] and identify the executive sponsor the DMBOK2 expects [DMBOK2-C03-02]. Lowest overhead; no layered escalation.

Option 2 - council-based escalation ladder: adopt the DMBOK2 pattern in which stewardship teams settle what they can, escalations are logged, and unresolved issues go up to a Data Governance Council and then to corporate governance or management [DMBOK2-C03-44, DMBOK2-C03-46], with the escalation procedure published [DMBOK2-C03-61]. Needs a council to exist; level names and members are shown in Table 4 and Figure 20, which are unverifiable from text.

Option 3 - council with delegated steering committee: as Option 2, but the council delegates enforcement of policies to a Data Stewardship Steering Committee [DMBOK2-C03-40], reflecting the DMBOK2 view that governance work is often divided among several committees with different purposes and levels of oversight [DMBOK2-C03-12]. Suits a larger programme than the project currently describes.

Option A - single accountable executive: name one senior executive as governance owner and escalation point, acting as sponsor for the capability. The DMBOK2 describes a single top accountable leader as making decisions easier and accountability clear, and names an executive sponsor (ideally the CDO) for oversight. Backed by DMBOK2-C16-10 and DMBOK2-C15-20.

Option B - decision-making governance forum: route escalations to a Data Governance Steering Committee with working groups, either newly created or an existing committee used cautiously, and require that it is a decision-making body. Backed by DMBOK2-C16-22, DMBOK2-C16-13 and DMBOK2-C16-23.

Option C - documented accountability map: keep the current structure and record Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed roles for Factory sign-off, operational sign-off and override authority in a RACI matrix, which the DMBOK2 presents as adding accountability without changing organisation charts. Backed by DMBOK2-C16-08 and DMBOK2-C16-09.

dmbok_terms: policy adoption by the Data Governance Council
positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 defines data policies as directives that turn principles and management intent into fundamental rules about what to do and not do, with standards and procedures describing how; policies are drafted by data management or policy staff, refined by stewards and management and adopted by the Data Governance Council, and must be communicated, monitored, enforced and re-evaluated, while data standards should be mandatory and reviewed, approved and adopted by the council or a delegated workgroup. It does not discuss who may interpret a policy or the risk of presenting an inferred rule as policy, which is a project-specific control.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md (non-goal of presenting inferred organisational policy as fact; 'policy interpretation where material' under human approval), README.md principle 2 (agents must not invent business definitions or policy) and the Definition & CDE contract (authoritative sources limited to named policy repositories; an 'approved' CDE-criteria document is required input). The stance that only governed documents carry policy authority agrees with the DMBOK2 adoption route. Rated Partial because the compared files use 'policy' as one undifferentiated term (no policy, standard and procedure distinction, and standards adoption is not in the human-approval list) and do not define 'authoritative' policy by its approval route beyond the contract's mention of an 'approved' document. Suggested wording: where policy is named, say 'policy and data standards adopted through the organisation's approval route', and keep the inferred-policy prohibition as a project-specific rule.
caveats: Chapter 3 is silent on interpretation of policy and on automated agents inferring policy, so the 'policy interpretation where material' gate and the inferred-policy ban have no DMBOK2 passage behind them.
The DMBOK2 notes that policies and standards vary widely between organisations; the adoption route it describes is a general pattern, and the organisation's own approval route takes precedence.

positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 says a governance programme must measure progress and success through metrics that show the business value delivered, and its sample metrics cover value (business objectives, risk reduction, operational efficiency), effectiveness (goals achieved, steward use of tools, communication and training, speed of adoption) and sustainability (performance of policies and processes, conformance to standards). An automated scorecard can report these to the council and steering committees and expose trends in issues by location and root cause, data quality measurement reports are among the content a programme publishes, and metrics are expected to change as the programme matures.

The DMBOK2 treats metrics as a core part of improvement and as a communications tool, expects each organisation to tailor them to its target-state roadmap, lists governance and metrics to measure progress among the contents of an assessment report, and asks that adoption of data management guidelines be measured. In these chapters the metrics are framed around maturity assessment and programme adoption, and no fixed format for a stewardship governance report is given.
rationales: Compared README.md ('governance reporting' is listed among steward responsibilities with no content, audience or cadence), HANDOFF.md 'Success criteria' (agents know their boundaries; humans know where accountability sits; claims traceable; assumptions visible; controls, mappings and lineage linked to meaning and impact; exceptions analysed as patterns; agents evaluated independently; governance applied to the agents) and docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md Phase 5 (agent behaviour scored on seven evaluation dimensions). These criteria test the AI-augmented system, not the value, effectiveness or sustainability of stewardship that DMBOK2 metrics address, and the compared files define no scorecard or metric set for governance reporting. Rated Partial rather than Missing because measurement artefacts exist but target a different object. Adopting any option is a human decision and the organisation's own governance metrics outrank the DMBOK2.

Compared README.md (Business context lists 'governance reporting' as a stewardship responsibility) and HANDOFF.md ('Success criteria'). No document defines the content, audience, cadence or measures of governance reporting, and the ten Success criteria are qualitative conditions (for example 'claims are traceable') rather than measures that can be reported and trended. The DMBOK2 pairs reporting with tailored metrics and progress measurement, which the project does not yet describe. Suggested wording: say what governance reporting covers, that its metrics are to be defined by the organisation (DMBOK2 sample metrics as general industry context only), and that the Success criteria are acceptance conditions for the system, not reporting metrics.
caveats: The conversion flattens the sample-metrics list (bullet levels are lost and 'Sustainability' appears as a stray heading), so the grouping into value, effectiveness and sustainability is read from layout.
Chapter 3 gives sample metrics only; it prescribes no particular KPIs, targets or reporting cadence.
Chapters 15-16 frame metrics around maturity assessment and programme adoption; metrics specific to data governance or data quality are probably covered in chapters outside this range.
proposal_options: Option 1 - adopt the DMBOK2 metric groups: structure governance reporting under value, effectiveness and sustainability headings, map the HANDOFF.md success criteria into effectiveness and sustainability, and add value measures (business objectives, risk reduction, operational efficiency) [DMBOK2-C03-65, DMBOK2-C03-66, DMBOK2-C03-67, DMBOK2-C03-68].

Option 2 - governance scorecard: define a periodic scorecard of governance activity and policy compliance, with issue trends by location and root cause, reported to the accountable governance body, and include data quality measurement reports [DMBOK2-C03-63, DMBOK2-C03-45, DMBOK2-C03-60].

Option 3 - defer and record: keep the HANDOFF.md success criteria as system-level criteria only, record that programme-level stewardship metrics are deferred to the organisation's own governance metrics, and revisit as the programme matures, since the DMBOK2 expects metrics to change with maturity [DMBOK2-C03-64].

positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 lists continuous improvement of data management processes among the principles of a data-centric organisation and describes governance as an ongoing process with no end date; it feeds improvement through stakeholder feedback, periodic re-evaluation of policies, and a community of interest in which practitioners learn from each other.

The DMBOK2 ties continuous improvement to a repeating cycle of baseline, scheduled re-assessment and trend tracking, and advises improving data management incrementally in line with business objectives. The term itself matches the project's usage; the chapters give no stewardship-specific improvement process.
rationales: Compared README.md, which lists 'continuous improvement' among the stewardship responsibilities. The statement and its wording match the DMBOK2 principle. No improvement mechanism (feedback loop, review cadence) is specified, but the README entry is a scope statement and does not claim one; the metrics proposal under A-06 would be the natural place to add it. Suggested citation: reference the DMBOK2 principle as general industry context where the responsibility is listed.

Compared README.md (Business context lists 'continuous improvement' as a stewardship responsibility) and HANDOFF.md (suggested sequence step 11, 'Iterate'). Nothing in the repository says how stewardship practice is reviewed or improved over time; step 11 concerns building the agents, not the stewardship practice. The term matches the DMBOK2, which however attaches it to a baseline and scheduled re-assessment that the project does not describe. Suggested wording: describe continuous improvement as periodic review of stewardship outcomes against a stated baseline, leaving the cycle options under A-32 for human decision.
caveats: The improvement principle is a single bullet in section 1.3.1 and the supporting mechanisms are spread across sections 2.7, 2.9 and 2.17; Chapter 3 describes no dedicated improvement process.
The DMBOK2 anchors continuous improvement in maturity re-assessment, so any improvement cycle proposed depends on the maturity-measure decision recorded under A-32.

positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 treats stakeholder involvement as part of stewardship: stewards surface rules until there is consensus, business stewards are typically recognised subject matter experts who work with stakeholders to define and control data, governance is made representative so all stakeholders can be heard, stewardship is described as collaborative, terminology approvers should include core user groups, and issue management documents stakeholder viewpoints and resolution alternatives.

The DMBOK2 defines stakeholders broadly, naming individual SMEs and internal groups such as operations, recommends analysing them early to decide how to engage them, and stresses explaining why each stakeholder's involvement matters; it names stewards, owners and custodians as the frontline roles needing deeper understanding of the initiative. It does not discuss routing unresolved questions to stakeholders.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md (objective: 'identify unresolved questions requiring SME or Data Owner input') and the Definition & CDE contract (conflicting internal sources are routed to the human steward rather than resolved; outputs include open_questions and human_action_required; no definition is invented from general knowledge). Seeking input from the people who hold the knowledge, and recording the open point instead of answering it, matches the DMBOK2 consensus-and-documentation view of rules and definitions. Suggested citation: reference the DMBOK2 stakeholder passages as general industry context where the SME and Data Owner question step is described.

Compared HANDOFF.md (objective list: agents 'identify unresolved questions requiring SME or Data Owner input') and README.md (the system is not intended to replace the Data Steward, Data Owner, SMEs, operational teams or governance forums). This fits the DMBOK2 emphasis on engaging stakeholders. However no stakeholders are identified: SMEs and Data Owners are unnamed, Phase 0b of docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md names only governance sign-off roles, and the Orchestrator's routing table is deferred, so agents have no stated destination for these questions and there is no analysis of whose input matters most. Suggested wording: state that questions go to named SMEs and Data Owners per domain once identified, and add them to the Phase 0b role-naming list; a stakeholder register is a possible later step.
caveats: The DMBOK2 speaks of stakeholders and business Data Stewards rather than 'SMEs' and 'operations teams'; its only reference close to operations teams is production support teams in the issue-management section.
The DMBOK2 passages describe human stakeholder processes; none addresses an automated agent raising questions for them.

In the DMBOK2 a Data Steward is usually itself a recognised subject matter expert (7.2.2), whereas the project treats SMEs as a separate source of input to the steward; the text does not contradict this but is less distinct.
The assigned chapters do not discuss routing unresolved questions to stakeholders, so the match is at the level of stakeholder engagement, not of the project's specific agent behaviour.

positions: General industry context: the DMBOK2 makes Data Stewards generally responsible for business glossary content, expects definitions to be clear and to explain exceptions, synonyms and variants, and says terminology approvers should include representatives of core user groups; it notes that drafts can come from another function such as Data Architecture and that each glossary term carries further metadata including the responsible steward. The glossary holds agreed-upon definitions, but this range prescribes no status model (such as draft, approved, retired) or approval workflow for definitions.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: The chapter says more mature metadata governance moves business terms and definitions through governed status changes, giving an example path from candidate term to approved, published, and finally replaced or retired; the data governance team manages the status changes and data stewards manage term lifecycles in the business glossary. It adds that developing business metadata requires stewardship, but it names no separate approving role.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md ('business definition approval' under human approval; autonomous approval of definitions is a non-goal) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (candidate definitions carry status DRAFT-NOT-APPROVED and a source-attribution rationale; 'Any candidate definition becoming final' needs human approval). Drafting by a supporting source and approval by a group that includes core user representatives is the pattern the DMBOK2 describes, and the project's draft-by-agent, approve-by-human split follows it. The project does not name who approves (the DMBOK2 asks for core user-group representatives among approvers); that gap sits under A-04. Suggested citation: reference the DMBOK2 glossary section as general industry context where the draft-and-approve rule is stated.

Compared HANDOFF.md ('business definition approval' under Human approval required) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (candidate_definitions carry status DRAFT-NOT-APPROVED; human_approval_required_for lists 'Any candidate definition becoming final'). The project already uses the DMBOK2's 'candidate' term and a human gate before a definition becomes final, but it specifies only that first gate: nothing names the approved, published or replaced/retired stages, so the approval lifecycle is only partly covered. The agent-drafts, human-approves split itself is an AI-specific control the DMBOK2 does not address.
caveats: Chapter 3 gives no lifecycle states or formal approval workflow for definitions; any such detail would be in chapters outside this reading unit.

The contract's candidate_definitions fields (term, draft_text, cited and paraphrased clauses, status) have no separate slots for synonyms, exceptions or variants, or for the responsible steward, which the DMBOK2 says definitions and glossary terms carry; these may sit in draft_text or in other output fields, so the point is noted but not scored.
The DMBOK2 gives the candidate, approved, published, replaced or retired path as an example and as a feature of more mature governance, not as a required set of states.
The chapter assigns status changes to the data governance team and names no separate approving role; approver roles are a Chapter 3 matter outside this unit.
AI agents drafting definitions is outside the 2017 text.
proposal_options: Adopt the DMBOK2 example status path (candidate, approved, published, replaced or retired) as the definition-status vocabulary in the Definition & CDE contract and any future definitions/ records, with a human approval gate on each change; costs a schema, contract and test update and a decision on who approves each transition (DMBOK2-C12-63, DMBOK2-C12-61).

Keep the single DRAFT-NOT-APPROVED gate in this repository and leave published and replaced or retired states to the status model of the glossary system once it is chosen, treating the DMBOK2 path as an example of more mature governance; costs nothing now but leaves later lifecycle stages undefined here (DMBOK2-C12-62, DMBOK2-C12-22).

positions: GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: Within reference and master data, Chapter 10 treats a definition as giving information that a code label cannot, and it shows both naming problems the project cares about: business units using different terms for one thing, and source systems using one attribute name for different things or several names for one enterprise attribute. It expects Data Stewards to work with the business to reconcile these and agree attribute naming and enterprise level definitions, balancing common wording against local flexibility and relating differing representations through cross-reference lists; 'synonym' appears only as synonym rings for search, and nothing in this range describes a business glossary as such.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: The business glossary stores business concepts, terminology, definitions and the relationships between terms, and its recommended attributes include synonyms, the unit responsible for the data, and conflicting definitions awaiting resolution, with reporting on pending and missing-definition items. Data stewards raise terminology issues and help resolve differences across the organisation, and the chapter prefers deliberately developed definitions to simply accepting existing ones because inconsistent definitions carry misuse risk.
rationales: Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Definition & CDE Agent: 'locate existing definitions', 'compare definitions', 'identify conflicts', 'identify synonyms', 'identify missing definitions'), HANDOFF.md ('business definitions, synonyms, terminology conflicts, ownership gaps') and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (responsible_for; the 'Get glossary term links' tool for term relationships and synonyms; the escalation rule that conflicting internal sources go to a human steward rather than being resolved by the agent). This matches the Chapter 10 practice, in which differences in terms and attribute names are surfaced and reconciled by Data Stewards working with the business; the agent only supports that work and its candidate definitions stay unapproved until a human decides. No essential Chapter 10 element is missing from the concept as stated, so the status is Aligned and the only action is a citation; 'synonyms' and 'terminology conflicts' are the project's own words and no wording change is proposed because the chapter's near-equivalents describe the same activity. The grade is provisional for the glossary as an artefact, which this chapter does not cover.

Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Definition & CDE Agent responsibilities: identify conflicts, synonyms, ownership gaps and missing definitions, and prepare candidate definitions for human review) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (same duties; internal sources that conflict are routed to the human steward). Each duty has a direct DMBOK2 counterpart (synonym attribute, conflicting-definition attribute, responsible-unit attribute, pending and missing-definition reporting) and resolution stays with a human steward as in the DMBOK2, so concept and wording align and a citation is the only change needed.
caveats: Chapter 10 does not describe a business glossary as an artefact; that treatment sits in a chapter outside this unit, so this grade reflects only the reference and master data view and is provisional for the glossary itself.

The chapter's one literal use of 'synonym' is 'synonym rings' as a search-and-discovery feature of Reference Data storage, and 'terminology conflict' is not its term; it speaks of different terms and attribute naming.

The chapter lists attributes a glossary should carry (acronym, categorisation, responsible unit, conflict nature and timeline, algorithms, lineage, authoritative source); the contract does not define the glossary's attribute set because no glossary system is selected, so attribute-level alignment cannot yet be judged.
The DMBOK2 does not discuss automated comparison or drafting of definitions.

positions: GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: The chapter separates the business glossary from the data dictionary (the structure and contents of the data sets in a database, application or warehouse, often fed by modelling tools) and from the directory or catalog (systems, sources and locations of data), and counts items such as physical table and column names as technical metadata, one of three metadata types. It says a dictionary helps stop meaning captured in logical models from being lost once physical structures go live, and that documentation of the metadata solution should include a master catalog of the sources and targets in scope.
rationales: Compared README.md ('data dictionaries' and 'documentation' in the stewardship scope list) and AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md (an 'approved internal data dictionary' and an 'approved metadata catalogue' as example authoritative sources). The responsibility is named and the dictionary is already treated as an authoritative input, but no file says what a data dictionary or documentation covers, how it differs from the business glossary and from a catalog, or which technical metadata the agents rely on; ARCHITECTURE.md gives no agent a dictionary duty and its Stewardship as Code artefact list has no dictionary or documentation class. This is a gap in terms and definitions rather than a conflict, so wording is the proportionate action.
caveats: The chapter attributes dictionary content mainly to database and modelling tools and asks stewards and other data management professionals to ensure maintenance processes exist; it names no role that writes or approves dictionary text.
In the chapter, documentation means documentation of the metadata solution (sources and targets in scope); README.md does not say which documentation it means.

positions: GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: The only related wording found in this chapter says a formal assessment of metadata maturity should include the critical business data elements alongside glossaries, lineage, profiling and data quality processes. The chapter does not define critical data elements, set criteria or a designation process, name who designates them, or describe the evidence needed.

DMBOK2 uses criticality to focus data quality work: data is judged against common drivers (regulatory reporting, financial reporting, business policy, ongoing operations, business strategy), Master Data counts as critical by definition, and data sets or elements are assessed through the processes and reports that consume them and the financial, regulatory or reputational risk if they fail, producing a ranked list for the Data Quality team. It says the drivers vary by industry, names data stewards and data owners as the people who identify critical data, and describes no formal designation or approval step in Chapter 13.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md ('CDE designation' under Human approval required) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (identifies CDE evidence; human approval for any CDE status designation; assumption that no approved CDE-criteria policy document is named yet). Chapter 12 gives nothing to test the designation gate, the evidence duty or the missing criteria document against, so on this chapter's text the DMBOK2 is silent; closing the criteria gap is a matter for internal policy, which outranks the DMBOK2, and criteria guidance may sit in chapters outside this unit.

Compared HANDOFF.md ('Human approval required' includes CDE designation), contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (the agent only gathers CDE evidence and lists an approved CDE-criteria policy as a required input) and docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md section 6 (CDE criteria must be a named source, not agent knowledge). Human designation with agent-gathered evidence is consistent with DMBOK2, where stewards and owners identify critical data. The gap is the criteria themselves: DMBOK2 treats a criticality assessment and ranked list as the basis for focusing quality work, but the project has no criteria document, and the contract's placeholder 'pending Phase 0b' has no matching item in docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md Phase 0b, which lists only accountable roles and the Data-Quality-Dimension taxonomy. Every option below is a proposal for the project owner to approve; internal policy outranks DMBOK2.
caveats: Status reflects Chapter 12 only: criteria and designation may be treated in chapters outside this unit, and a real status from those units should take precedence.
The only related wording found in this chapter is 'critical business data elements' in the readiness-assessment section.
DMBOK2 says criticality drivers differ by industry, so its list is a common starting set and not a standard (DMBOK2-C13-04).
Chapter 13 gives no designation or approval procedure for critical data and names no approving role; the project's human-designation rule is consistent with, but not stated in, the chapter.
Terminology: Chapter 13 defines 'Critical Data'; the phrase 'critical data elements' occurs once, in the discussion of what measurements should cover (DMBOK2-C13-33).

Footnote 73, collected with the other footnotes at the end of the chapter (matched by footnote order), cites Jugulum (2014), chapters 6 and 7, for rationalising critical data; that source is not in the supplied text.
proposal_options: Criticality drivers as the starting checklist: draft the CDE-criteria policy around the DMBOK2 common drivers (data required for regulatory reporting, financial reporting, business policy, ongoing operations or business strategy; Master Data critical by definition), assessed through consuming processes, the reports the data appears in, and financial, regulatory or reputational risk. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-05, DMBOK2-C13-06 and DMBOK2-C13-07; DMBOK2-C13-04 notes the drivers vary by industry, so the organisation would tailor the list.

Leaner prioritisation factors: start with the three factors DMBOK2 uses for ranking (regulatory requirements, financial value, direct impact on customers) and make a ranked list of data the policy's output. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-23 and DMBOK2-C13-24. Simpler to approve first time, but it omits the business-policy, ongoing-operations and strategy drivers in the first option.

Policy form: whichever criteria set is chosen, record it in a governed Data Quality policy using the DMBOK2 policy outline (purpose, scope and applicability; definitions; responsibilities; reporting; implementation) rather than leaving the criteria inside the agent contract. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-60, with DMBOK2-C13-59 for who identifies critical data.

positions: GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: The chapter treats metadata as data that must itself be managed: start from a strategy and requirements before choosing products, then build a metamodel, keep current, planned and historical versions, assign formal metadata roles with stewards making sure maintenance processes exist, and avoid creating metadata for its own sake. It describes centralized, distributed and hybrid repository architectures with different trade-offs, says the choice depends on organisational requirements, and warns about duplicated repositories.
rationales: Compared ARCHITECTURE.md ('Long-term concept: Stewardship as Code': structured, version-controlled governance artefacts where that improves traceability, testing or change-impact analysis, explicitly not every document) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (read-only access to an external glossary/catalog system that is not yet selected). The intent matches the DMBOK2 (metadata managed as versioned data and not created for its own sake), but the project uses its own term, states no metadata strategy or metamodel, and does not say which store is authoritative for each artefact class, so a repository-held definitions/ folder and an external glossary could become the duplicate stores the DMBOK2 warns about.
caveats: Stewardship as Code is a project term with no DMBOK2 equivalent; mapping it to a metadata repository with versioning is by analogy.
The DMBOK2 says the architecture choice depends on organisational requirements and does not rank centralized, distributed and hybrid.

The chapter recommends open relational database platforms for repositories, whereas the project's examples are folders of version-controlled files; this is an implementation difference the owner may wish to note rather than a conflict.
proposal_options: Hybrid: keep the version-controlled repository for steward-added governance metadata only (candidate and approved definitions, CDE evidence, decisions, links) and point to the glossary, catalog and source systems for everything else; costs a link convention and the effort of joining repository entries with source results at query time (DMBOK2-C12-41, DMBOK2-C12-42).

Centralized: treat the repository as the single store holding copies of governance metadata taken from the source systems, giving one searchable store; costs the replication processes needed to keep copies current, and the DMBOK2 notes that teams with limited IT resources or seeking maximum automation may avoid it (DMBOK2-C12-36, DMBOK2-C12-37, DMBOK2-C12-38).

Distributed: hold no copies in the repository and have agents read the authoritative systems on demand, recording only references; metadata is retrieved from its source at the time of use, but there is no place for steward-added or manual entries (DMBOK2-C12-39, DMBOK2-C12-40).

positions: GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: The chapter treats provenance as metadata about data: provenance and lineage are business metadata, a glossary term can record the official or authoritative source behind its data, maintenance requirements include logging updates and referring them for approval, and a staging area gives an interim audit trail for investigating source or quality issues. It also warns that reusing existing definitions is risky when the care behind them is unknown, but it does not classify claims by kind of evidence or address machine-generated claims.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md (Evidence policy: authoritative internal evidence, general industry context, agent inference, open question, human decision required) and schemas/evidence.schema.json (authority_level: authoritative_internal, general_industry, inferred; direct_or_inferred; source_id, location and timestamp). The underlying idea of traceable provenance matches the DMBOK2 but under different terms, while the five-way separation of claims is an AI-specific control with no DMBOK2 counterpart, so it should be recorded as a deliberate deviation rather than changed.
caveats: The project's categories apply to agent claims, whereas DMBOK2 provenance applies to data and metadata, so the mapping is by analogy.
The DMBOK2 (2017) is silent on confidence labelling and evidence classification of machine-generated output.

evidence.schema.json authority_level has three values; the other two HANDOFF.md categories (open question, human decision required) are carried in separate output fields of the contract, which is a project matter rather than a DMBOK2 one.

positions: The DMBOK2 describes lineage as documentation of how data is acquired or created and where it moves and changes, adds that detailed lineage records the change rules and their frequency, treats data flows as a form of lineage documentation, and says custom ETL and legacy data-manipulation objects should be documented so the impact of flow changes can be analysed. It calls forward and backward lineage critical to impact analysis, lists determining lineage impact among data-architecture activities that keep business rules along a flow consistent and traceable, makes governance responsible for keeping knowledge of data origins and movement documented, and notes that emerging compliance standards expect organisations to explain where data originated and how it changed.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: The chapter classes lineage documentation, including upstream and downstream change impact, as technical metadata and presents lineage and impact analysis as a technique for showing how data is transformed between systems: lineage read from code ('as implemented') and lineage read from mapping specifications ('as designed') are connected by 'stitching', ideally from the official source or system of record to the final destination, and any lineage is limited by the coverage of the metadata system. It offers a business-focused discovery strategy that limits scope to business-prioritised data elements and a technical-focused one that starts at source systems and repeatedly identifies consumers, the latter suited to impact questions such as which systems a column change affects.
rationales: ARCHITECTURE.md gives the Mapping & Lineage Agent source-target mapping analysis, lineage completeness, dependency mapping and downstream impact, and HANDOFF.md's success criteria require lineage to be linkable to downstream impact; together these cover the lineage-documentation and impact-analysis activities the DMBOK2 describes. The gap is wording only: the project names the downstream direction, while the DMBOK2 pairs forward and backward lineage and separates high-level from detailed lineage, which the project text leaves implicit. Proposed wording (for human approval): name both forward and backward lineage and say whether high-level or detailed lineage is expected.

Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Mapping & Lineage Agent: lineage completeness, dependency mapping, downstream impact) and HANDOFF.md (AI may identify missing lineage). The concept matches the DMBOK2 lineage and impact-analysis technique; only the vocabulary differs (completeness and downstream impact versus coverage, stitching, as-implemented and as-designed lineage, and impact analysis). Defining 'lineage completeness' with the DMBOK2 coverage limit and the as-implemented/as-designed distinction would make it testable. No Mapping & Lineage contract exists yet, so the comparison is at architecture-description level.
caveats: 'Lineage completeness' has no counterpart term in the DMBOK2 text read, and no completeness measure is defined there; alignment is judged on documented lineage and impact analysis, not on the term.
Chapter 12 (Metadata) is the DMBOK2's main treatment of lineage as metadata and lies outside this unit (read in unit 5); this row rests on Chapters 4 and 8 only.
The chapter assumes tool-extracted lineage and does not discuss AI-assisted lineage analysis.
The two lineage diagrams (Figures 89 and 90) are missing from the text; the claims here rest on the surrounding prose only.

positions: The DMBOK2 describes mapping as specifying the rules for transforming data from one location and format to another, covering targets, update rules and any transformation rules or calculations, and names semantic conversion as a transformation whose purpose is to keep the meaning of data values consistent. It treats these rules as a business matter: metadata is expected to track business meaning, transformation rules and lineage together and to record business as well as technical definitions of the data and its transformation, business stakeholders should approve changes to the rules, mapping designs and changes should be reviewed with business subject matter experts in each involved system, and a purely technical approach is said to invite errors in mappings and transformations; separately, models are mapped across levels of the enterprise data model, which creates model lineage.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: Source-to-target mapping documentation is classed as technical metadata and transformation rules, calculations and derivations as business metadata; mapping repositories are described as adding version control and change analysis, and lineage read from mapping specifications is the 'as designed' view, distinct from the 'as implemented' view in code. The chapter also notes that meaning captured in logical models is often lost when physical structures go live and lists the algorithms behind a definition as a glossary attribute, but it states no test that meaning survives a transformation.
rationales: The Mapping & Lineage Agent's key question in ARCHITECTURE.md ('Did the meaning survive the transformation?'), together with its source-target mapping analysis, transformation identification and mapping-definition consistency responsibilities, is the concern the DMBOK2 addresses through semantic conversion and business review of mappings; HANDOFF.md's success criterion that mappings can be linked back to meaning is in the same spirit as the DMBOK2's cross-level model mapping. The project leaves mapping-specification contents and the approver of mapping-rule changes to the organisation's own process, and HANDOFF.md reserves production changes and governance decisions to humans, which is consistent with the DMBOK2 placing approval with business stakeholders. Proposed citation (general industry context): reference the semantic conversion and mapping-review passages where the key question is stated.

Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Mapping & Lineage Agent: source-target mapping analysis, transformation identification, mapping-definition consistency; key question 'Did the meaning survive the transformation?') and AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md ('approved mapping specification' as an example authoritative source). Treating mappings and transformation rules as governed metadata and checking them against definitions is consistent with the DMBOK2 treatment of mapping documentation, transformation rules and algorithm-linked definitions. The key question is a project framing the chapter does not state, so alignment is at concept level and a citation is enough; the as-designed versus as-implemented point that could sharpen the question is carried on A-15.
caveats: The DMBOK2 text read gives no test for whether meaning has been preserved; 'did the meaning survive the transformation' is the project's framing, which the semantic conversion example supports only in spirit.

HANDOFF.md's human-approval list does not name changes to mapping or transformation rules explicitly (production changes and governance decisions cover them by implication), whereas the DMBOK2 places approval of such changes with business stakeholders.

No Chapter 12 passage states a meaning-preservation test; the DMBOK2 supplies ingredients only (mapping specifications, transformation rules, algorithms attached to definitions, designed versus implemented lineage).
Statements about mapping tools reflect 2017 vendor capabilities.

dmbok_terms: Chain of dependencies between business capabilities
positions: The DMBOK2 does not use the term data contract; its nearest constructs are the data sharing agreement or memorandum of understanding, to be agreed before interfaces are built, approved by the business data stewards of the data and specifying anticipated use, access, restrictions and expected service levels, and an agreed exchange format or data layout between systems. It treats dependencies as business capabilities that need data other capabilities produce, as process dependencies that the target load process must monitor, and as lineage knowledge that sharing agreements rely on to know where data moves and persists.

Chapter 13 does not use the term data contract; its nearest constructs are the data quality Service Level Agreement, which records an organisation's expectations for response and remediation per system, and a passing reference to a data sharing agreement. Upstream dependency appears as a recognised cause of quality issues (source systems changing structure without telling downstream consumers) and as a practice (making staff in upstream systems aware of their impact on downstream users).
rationales: README.md lists data contracts and upstream dependency management as stewardship responsibilities; ARCHITECTURE.md names data-contracts/ only as a possible Stewardship-as-Code directory and gives the Mapping & Lineage Agent dependency mapping (and the Exception & Root-Cause Agent 'identify common upstream dependencies'); BUILD-BACKLOG.md lists 'data contract generation' as future work; AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md lets an agent treat an 'approved data contract' as authoritative. No repository artefact says what a data contract contains or who approves it, and 'upstream dependency management' is not a defined activity, so the concept is present but under-specified and uses a term the DMBOK2 does not, whereas the DMBOK2 data sharing agreement has stated contents and business data steward approval. Proposed wording (for human approval): note that 'data contract' corresponds to what the DMBOK2 calls a data sharing agreement plus exchange specification (general industry context), and use the DMBOK2 contents as a checklist when the data-contracts/ artefact is first designed.

Compared README.md (lists 'data contracts' and 'upstream dependency management' as stewardship responsibilities), ARCHITECTURE.md (a possible data-contracts/ folder under 'Stewardship as Code'), BUILD-BACKLOG.md ('data contract generation' in the future backlog) and AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md ('approved data contract' as an example authoritative source). The concept is present but only as a named responsibility and in a term Chapter 13 does not use, and the reviewed passages do not say what a contract contains, who agrees it or how upstream change reaches the steward; DMBOK2's SLA contents and upstream-awareness practices cover those elements. Suggested wording change: where README.md and BUILD-BACKLOG.md name data contracts, add a note that the nearest DMBOK2 Chapter 13 constructs are the data quality SLA and the data sharing agreement, labelled as general industry context.
caveats: 'Data contract' and 'upstream dependency management' are not DMBOK2 terms in the text read; treating the data sharing agreement and the data exchange specification as the closest constructs is the reader's interpretation and needs human confirmation.
The DMBOK2 handles dependencies as architecture, integration and lineage-impact concerns rather than as a named stewardship activity, so no single passage matches 'upstream dependency management'.
'Data contract' is not a Chapter 13 term; relating it to the data quality SLA or the data sharing agreement is by analogy and is a reviewer judgement.
Chapter 13 mentions 'data sharing agreement' once, in the discussion of metric trending, and does not define it (DMBOK2-C13-55).

positions: DMBOK2 defines a Data Quality dimension as a measurable feature of data that provides the vocabulary for stating requirements and measuring results, and presents four published sets (Strong-Wang's 15 dimensions in four categories, Redman's groups for data model, data values and representation, English's inherent versus pragmatic split, and DAMA UK's six core dimensions) while stating that no single set is agreed. It advises expressing rules in terms of dimensions applied consistently, and notes that some dimensions are objectively measurable while others rest on context or subjective interpretation.
rationales: Compared docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md (Data Quality Agent section 8 and Open Question 5) and docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md (Phase 0b item 2), which both state that no approved, versioned Data-Quality-Dimension taxonomy exists and make it a blocking prerequisite, and ARCHITECTURE.md, which has the Data Quality Agent 'identify relevant quality dimension'. DMBOK2 treats dimensions as the core vocabulary for rules and measurement, so the absent artefact is a gap. The project's direction matches DMBOK2: the organisation approves its own set and industry dimensions are not presented as internal policy, and the six names in Phase 0b equal the DAMA UK six. Every option below is a proposal for the project owner to approve; internal policy outranks DMBOK2.
caveats: unverifiable from text: Table 29 (Common Dimensions of Data Quality, with definitions and measurement approaches, PDF pages 754-756) and Figure 92 (relationships between dimensions, pages 757-758) are images that did not convert, so DMBOK2's consolidated definitions cannot be checked here.
DMBOK2 states there is no single agreed set of dimensions, so any choice is a judgement for the organisation (DMBOK2-C13-14).
DMBOK2 says some dimensions can be measured objectively while others depend on context or subjective interpretation (DMBOK2-C13-15).
proposal_options: DAMA UK core six: use completeness, uniqueness, timeliness, validity, accuracy and consistency as the starting set for the organisation's own versioned taxonomy; these are the examples docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md Phase 0b item 2 already names. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-12; DMBOK2-C13-13 shows DAMA UK keeps other quality characteristics outside the six, so the taxonomy would need to say where those sit.

English inherent/pragmatic split: organise the taxonomy in two tiers, inherent characteristics versus pragmatic ones, so dimensions that do not depend on data use are kept apart from those that do, which fits the project's fitness-for-purpose principle. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-11.

Strong-Wang consumer-perception set: adopt the 15 dimensions in four categories if the organisation wants dimensions framed around how data consumers perceive quality; it is a larger set, and DMBOK2-C13-15 warns that some dimensions rest on context or subjective interpretation. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-09.

Redman data-structure set: adopt Redman's grouping (data model, data values, representation) only if the taxonomy must also cover the quality of the model and of how data is recorded, not just stored values. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-10.

Own set with mapping: define an organisation-specific set and record a mapping to the published sets, relying on DMBOK2's statement that no single set is agreed and applying the chosen dimensions consistently in rules. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-14 and DMBOK2-C13-30.

dmbok_terms: business rule types (for example definitional conformance)
positions: DMBOK2 describes data quality business rules as statements of how data should exist to be usable, alignable with quality dimensions, and lists simple rule types (definitional conformance, value presence and completeness, format, value domain, range, mapping, consistency, accuracy, uniqueness and timeliness) plus aggregate checks. It says rules should be formulated consistently from templates, defined through dimensions, tested against actual data and confirmed by subject-matter experts, and that undocumented rules often have to be discovered.
rationales: Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Data Quality Agent: identify the quality dimension, propose a rule and a deterministic test, draft candidate SQL, flag the required threshold, link the test to the business definition) and HANDOFF.md (candidates only; approved requirements are the input; no business thresholds). That matches the DMBOK2 flow from business expectation to rule and keeps SME confirmation with humans. Missing against DMBOK2 sections 1.3.7, 2.7.1 and 3.4: no rule-type vocabulary, no standard template for documenting rules, no stated step in the passages reviewed where a candidate rule is tested against actual data before approval (docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md describes the SQL as draft and unexecuted), and no path for discovering rules that are not documented. The dimension link also depends on the unapproved taxonomy (A-18). Every option below is a proposal for the project owner to approve; internal policy outranks DMBOK2.
caveats: unverifiable from text: Table 30 (DQ Metric Examples, which shows example rules written in the chapter's pattern) is an image that did not convert, and the text gives no template layout.

DMBOK2 notes that rules are often undocumented and must be discovered (DMBOK2-C13-25), whereas the project's Data Quality Agent starts only from approved expectations; this is a difference of starting point, not a conflict.
proposal_options: Rule-type field: add a rule_type vocabulary taken from DMBOK2's simple business rule types (definitional conformance, value presence and record completeness, format compliance, value domain membership, range conformance, mapping conformance, consistency, accuracy verification, uniqueness verification, timeliness validation) so every candidate rule is classified, with definitional conformance tying a test back to the business definition. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-18 and DMBOK2-C13-19.

Pre-approval checklist: have each candidate rule carry the DMBOK2 rule-management attributes the project does not yet require (consistent documentation from a template, expressed through an approved dimension, tested against actual data, confirmed by subject-matter experts) before it reaches the Data Steward. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-30, DMBOK2-C13-31, DMBOK2-C13-32 and DMBOK2-C13-49.

Rule-discovery intake (optional): add a separately labelled path for rules inferred from processes or data rather than taken from an approved expectation, always tagged as agent inference needing SME confirmation, instead of leaving undocumented rules unaddressed. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-25 and DMBOK2-C13-32.

dmbok_terms: adoption of standards by the Data Governance Council
positions: General industry context: in Chapter 3 data quality standards are part of what governance sets and enforces, stewards help surface data quality rules until there is consensus about them, standards are reviewed, approved and adopted by the Data Governance Council or a delegated workgroup, rules, measurement methodologies and remediation standards are among the things to standardise, and a sample policy has a governance office certify data for use. The chapter does not use the term 'threshold' and does not discuss accepting data-quality risk.

DMBOK2 places threshold-setting with the business: acceptability thresholds are defined by business clients, metrics are approved by key stakeholders such as business owners and Data Stewards, and the business data owner is accountable. When an issue is found the Data Quality team confers with business data owners on how to resolve it, and taking no action because correction costs more than it is worth is a recognised option.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md (human approval for 'quality thresholds' and 'acceptance of data-quality risk'; non-goal of changing production quality thresholds; the Data Quality Agent 'must not set business thresholds') and docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md Phase 0b (an approved Data-Quality-Dimension taxonomy before the Data Quality Agent). The direction agrees with the DMBOK2: quality rules and standards are agreed with stakeholders and adopted by a governing body, and certification of data for use is a governance-office act. Rated Partial because the two decision types use terms that Chapter 3 does not name (threshold, risk acceptance), so alignment rests on mapping them to rules, standards and certification. Suggested wording: state that thresholds are parameters of data quality rules or standards adopted through the organisation's approval route, and keep 'acceptance of data-quality risk' as a project term.

Compared HANDOFF.md ('Human approval required' lists quality thresholds and acceptance of data-quality risk) and ARCHITECTURE.md (the Data Quality Agent is prohibited from setting business thresholds or approving controls). Keeping both decisions with humans matches DMBOK2, where the business defines thresholds and the business data owner is accountable. The project does not yet name which human role approves (docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md Phase 0b item 1 addresses roles), which belongs to the roles concepts rather than this one. Suggested citation: cite DMBOK2 Chapter 13 (acceptability thresholds, accountable business data owner) as general industry context where HANDOFF.md states these decisions.
caveats: Chapter 3 contains no passage on thresholds or on accepting data-quality risk; treating a threshold as part of a data quality rule or standard is an inference, and detailed guidance, if any, would be in chapters not read for this unit.
The sample policies in section 2.7, including the certification example, illustrate possible policy shapes and are not requirements.

DMBOK2 does not use the phrase 'acceptance of data-quality risk'; the nearest text is the 'taking no action' remediation option decided with business data owners (DMBOK2-C13-39, DMBOK2-C13-40), so the mapping is an inference.
Chapter 13 names business clients, key stakeholders and the accountable business data owner but gives no sign-off procedure for a threshold.

positions: DMBOK2 treats measurement and monitoring as core Data Quality operations: measurements inform data consumers (focused on critical data elements and relationships) and manage risk (relationships that failed before and similar functions), are built into the processing flow at element, record or data-set level, and are reported through scorecards and trends. SLAs state which data elements are covered and the expected quality per element, dimension and system; the chapter does not use the term control coverage or describe a coverage analysis.
rationales: Compared BUILD-BACKLOG.md, where 'control coverage analysis' appears only in the future backlog ('Each item must pass through the Agent Factory before implementation'), and docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md section 9, which notes that no production pipeline is named to run approved quality tests and persist exception records. The documents reviewed do not describe how quality is measured, monitored or reported, or what coverage would mean, while DMBOK2 treats measuring, monitoring and reporting as core Data Quality operations. The deferral is deliberate and visible in the backlog, so this is a known gap rather than an oversight. Every option below is a proposal for the project owner to approve; internal policy outranks DMBOK2.
caveats: unverifiable from text: Table 31 (Data Quality Monitoring Techniques, PDF page 793) and Table 30 (DQ Metric Examples, pages 791-792) are images that did not convert, so the specific monitoring techniques and metric layouts cannot be assessed.
'Control coverage' is not a DMBOK2 term; the coverage ideas in the options are inferred from the SLA scoping list and the guidance on where to place measurements.
proposal_options: Coverage matrix from the SLA scoping list: define coverage as, for each critical data element, which dimensions have an approved rule and threshold in which systems of the data value chain, mirroring the DMBOK2 SLA list of covered elements and per-element, per-dimension, per-system expectations. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-46 and DMBOK2-C13-33.

Risk-led coverage: prioritise gaps where relationships have failed before and where similar functions exist, following DMBOK2's guidance on where to place measurements. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-34 and DMBOK2-C13-33.

Measurement-level attribute: record for each control whether it measures at data element, record or data-set level, so coverage reports can show gaps by measurement level. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-36 (the technique table behind this, Table 31, is not in the text).

dmbok_terms: diagnosing issues, formulating options for remediation, resolving issues
standard vocabulary for data quality issues
positions: DMBOK2 expects operational procedures to diagnose each issue (symptoms, lineage, origin), formulate remediation options and resolve them in consultation with business data owners, with decisions kept in an incident tracking system (issue description, root causes, options, decision) and a standard issue vocabulary that also makes patterns and interdependencies across systems visible. It adds escalation based on impact, duration or urgency and issue metrics counted by dimension, business function and status.
rationales: Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Exception & Root-Cause Agent: cluster exceptions, identify recurring characteristics, correlate failures with source or process changes, propose hypotheses; barred from declaring root cause without sufficient evidence or resolving incidents directly) and HANDOFF.md (AI may cluster recurring exceptions; resolving operational incidents is a non-goal). Diagnosing and routing for a human decision fits DMBOK2, and the 'route for human decision' step corresponds to confirming with business data owners. The project does not yet define an issue record, an issue classification vocabulary, assignment, escalation or status tracking; docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md Open Question 6 (structure of exception records) is the closest open item. Every option below is a proposal for the project owner to approve; internal policy outranks DMBOK2.
caveats: The DMBOK2 procedures are written for a Data Quality team that also implements resolutions; the project deliberately keeps operational incident resolution with operations teams, so that part is a role difference rather than a conflict.
Chapter 13 does not describe automated clustering of exceptions; it relies on a standard classification vocabulary, so the project's clustering step is an extension rather than a DMBOK2 practice.
proposal_options: Minimum issue record: give the packet routed to a human the fields DMBOK2 lists for tracked issues (issue description, root causes, remediation options, decision), with the decision owner being a business data owner. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-41 and DMBOK2-C13-40.

Standard vocabulary and clustering keys: adopt a controlled issue classification (related to docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md Open Question 6 on exception structure) and use DMBOK2's issue metrics as clustering and reporting keys: dimension, business function, status, priority and severity, time to resolve. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-42, DMBOK2-C13-43 and DMBOK2-C13-61.
Escalation rule: define routing urgency by the impact, duration and urgency of an issue rather than by agent judgement. Backed by DMBOK2-C13-44.

dmbok_terms: hypotheses about root causes of data issues
positions: DMBOK2 defines a root cause as a factor whose removal would remove the problem, notes that issues often have several causes, and treats root-cause hypotheses as an assessment step to be confirmed with Data Stewards, SMEs and data consumers, stating that root-cause analysis needs technical and business SME input with the Data Quality team leading or facilitating. It lists Pareto analysis, fishbone diagrams, track and trace, process analysis and the Five Whys as common techniques and links pattern recognition to a standardised issue vocabulary.
rationales: Compared README.md (lists root-cause analysis and recurring quality-pattern identification as stewardship responsibilities), HANDOFF.md (AI may produce root-cause hypotheses; final root-cause determination where evidence is incomplete needs human approval), ARCHITECTURE.md (the Exception & Root-Cause Agent proposes hypotheses and the evidence needed to confirm them, and may not declare a root cause without sufficient evidence) and docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md section 9 (every hypothesis must cite its evidence). This matches DMBOK2, which treats root causes as hypotheses confirmed with stewards and SMEs. The project's qualifier 'where evidence is incomplete' is narrower than DMBOK2's expectation of SME input throughout, so reviewers may wish to confirm the intent. Suggested citation: cite DMBOK2 sections 2.4, 2.7.3 and 4.6 as general industry context for the hypothesis-and-confirmation approach.
caveats: DMBOK2 defines a root cause but gives no test for when evidence is sufficient; the project's sufficient-evidence standard remains its own.
