DMBOK2 expects SME input and confirmation throughout root-cause analysis, whereas HANDOFF.md reserves final human determination for cases where evidence is incomplete; the two are compatible but the project wording is narrower.

dmbok_terms: meets the expectations and needs of data consumers
positions: DMBOK2 defines data quality as the degree to which data meets the expectations and needs of its consumers, that is, whether it is fit for the purposes they apply it to, so quality depends on context and measurement should be developed against known uses and measurable rules. It warns that many organisations never define what makes data fit for purpose and that consumers' quality expectations are often not known.
rationales: Compared README.md, which lists 'data quality and fitness-for-purpose' among the stewardship responsibilities. The project's stance that quality is judged against purpose matches the DMBOK2 definition. The README passage does not say how purposes and consumer expectations are captured; DMBOK2 flags that as the usual weak point, which is useful context rather than a divergence. Suggested citation: cite DMBOK2 section 1.3.1 as general industry context where README.md names fitness-for-purpose.
caveats: DMBOK2 says expectations related to quality are not always known (DMBOK2-C13-03), so purposes have to be elicited from consumers rather than assumed.
DMBOK2 gives no test of 'fit' beyond requirement-based measurement through dimensions and rules.

dmbok_terms: Match, merge, survivorship and trust rules
positions: In Chapters 4 and 8 the DMBOK2 does not describe reference or master data stewardship itself (Chapter 10 does, and is read in unit 4); it treats master data as a first-order architecture and integration concern: capabilities that depend on nothing else constitute master data, enterprise data architecture typically starts with master data areas, integration is described as critical to reference data and master data management, and master data is to be processed before the transactional data that uses it. It names master data management hubs as a kind of data hub, lists match, merge, survivorship and trust rules as the business rules specific to master data management, and says a business analyst or data steward can extract business rules from existing documentation or system code.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: Chapter 10 presents Reference and Master Data as shared resources that need both governance and stewardship: stewards keep reference values complete and current and their definitions clear, either maintaining them directly or facilitating, and matching and merging tools still rely on stewards for exceptions and process improvement. It says use of transactional data depends on the quality of this data, that this data supplies the context in which transactions arrive, and that Master Data programmes should begin with one data domain and a handful of attributes.
rationales: ARCHITECTURE.md lists trading, orders, executions, transactions, positions, TBOR, IBOR, ABOR, valuation, NAV, reconciliation, regulatory reporting, enterprise data products and relevant source platforms as possible Context Agent content areas, and no project design, contract, schema or evaluation file mentions reference data or master data. The DMBOK2 treats both as managed parts of data management that architecture and integration must serve, so the absence of any stewardship artefact is a gap rather than an alignment. The status is provisional until merged with unit 4, which reads the DMBOK2's own reference and master data chapter.

Compared ARCHITECTURE.md, where 'reconciliation' appears once, as a possible content area of the Investment Operations Context Agent next to transactions, positions, valuation and NAV, and ran a keyword search of the repository's Markdown, contracts, schemas and agent files for reference data, master data and related terms, which found no reference or master data stewardship artefact (no register, role, contract section, schema field or backlog item). Chapter 10 treats stewardship of Reference and Master Data as part of data stewardship, so this is a coverage gap rather than a difference in wording; in my reading, Context-agent domain content does not stand in for the steward-held metadata, change control and coverage checks the chapter describes. The owner could instead record a deliberate exclusion from the initial scope (record-deviation); a structural proposal is offered because the chapter ties transaction-data quality to this data and gives scoping alternatives the owner can choose between.
caveats: Chapter 10 (Reference and Master Data) is outside this unit; the passages cited treat master and reference data as inputs to architecture and integration design and do not describe stewardship duties for them, so the status and options are provisional pending unit 4.

The master data example in the roadmap discussion rests partly on Figure 27 (missing from the converted text); only the one prose sentence quoted is relied on, and the example itself is unverifiable from text.

In Chapter 10 'reconciliation' means reconciling and consolidating data across sources into a master record; ARCHITECTURE.md lists 'reconciliation' as a possible Context-agent content area without defining it, so the two uses should not be assumed to be the same activity.
Table 23 (Critical Reference Data Metadata Attributes) is a missing figure, so its full attribute list is unverifiable from text; option 1 relies on the text list in section 2.2.5.

The chapter describes organisation-wide MDM and RDM programmes and tooling; it does not say how much applies to a stewardship function supported by AI agents, so the options are proposals for human decision, not DMBOK2 requirements.
proposal_options: Name reference data and master data as explicit content areas of the Investment Operations Context Agent, with no new agent or artefact type, in line with the DMBOK2 view that architecture typically starts with master data areas [DMBOK2-C04-17] and that integration is critical to reference and master data management [DMBOK2-C08-02]; this is the cheapest change but gives stewards context about the data, not stewardship of it.

Add a reference-and-master-data register as a Stewardship-as-Code artefact that names each data hub and the match, merge, survivorship and trust rules governing it, using the DMBOK2 hub and master data rule vocabulary [DMBOK2-C08-08] [DMBOK2-C08-20]; this brings the data itself under steward review and human approval but needs an owner and upkeep that the project has not assigned.

Reference Data first: add a small versioned register of the Reference Data sets that matter to Investment Operations, recording for each the steward name, originating organisation, update frequency and schedule, and the processes that use it, starting with the most important sets and leaving the owner to choose whether the steward maintains values directly or facilitates others (backed by DMBOK2-C10-34, DMBOK2-C10-30, DMBOK2-C10-32 and DMBOK2-C10-33); this is a governance document rather than a new agent, and its cost is a human-maintained register.

One Master Data domain first: choose a single Investment Operations master data domain, begin with a handful of attributes, and define who reviews match-and-merge exceptions as a steward task before any tooling is considered (backed by DMBOK2-C10-21 and DMBOK2-C10-29); the cost is a deeper stewardship commitment for one domain, with matching, merging and the choice of system of record staying with the Data Steward and the appropriate human owner.

Context-agent scope only: name reference data and master data as content areas of the Investment Operations Context Agent in ARCHITECTURE.md, keep the INTERNAL DOCUMENTED POSITION and GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT distinction, and define the project's use of 'reconciliation' so it is not confused with consolidating source records (backed by DMBOK2-C10-08, DMBOK2-C10-01 and DMBOK2-C10-22); this is the cheapest change but defines no stewardship duties, register or coverage check, so the gap stays partly open.

positions: The DMBOK2 text read says only that, when data is reused, the system of record or other authoritative data should be enforced, and that accuracy can be assessed only against a definitive set of data already determined to be correct. It also asks that existing system documentation be evaluated for accuracy and completeness and observes that real data always differs from what is assumed; it offers information on securities and their prices as a common example of data-as-a-service, but says nothing on how an AI assistant should rank internal documentation against general knowledge.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: Chapter 10 separates a System of Record (where data is created or maintained under defined rules) from a System of Reference (where consumers obtain reliable data even if it originated elsewhere), says each Master Data subject area will likely have its own system of record and that values should be replicated only from it, and describes a Trusted Source as the best version available, built from rules plus manual stewardship, while warning against overclaiming that data is 'golden'. It treats industry reference data as produced outside the organisation yet needed to understand its transactions, notes that the organisation's reconciled record can depart from an external directory while staying traceable to the contributing sources, asks that internal sources be identified, compared and assessed, and suggests a data sharing hub where no clear system of record exists.

GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT: Authority appears on the data side: the system of record for each data element is designated as business metadata, a glossary term can carry the official or authoritative source for the data behind it, and lineage is traced from the official source or system of record to the final destination. The chapter warns that reusing existing definitions is risky when the care behind them is unknown, but it neither ranks internal positions above industry guidance nor discusses naming authoritative evidence sources for AI agents.
rationales: The principle that authoritative sources outrank general knowledge is present in README.md (principle 3), in ARCHITECTURE.md's INTERNAL DOCUMENTED POSITION label, in the Authoritative Sources section required by AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md and in the internal-only authoritative_sources list of contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json, and it fits the DMBOK2 preference for authoritative data. It differs in object and term: the project ranks approved documents and registers as evidence for agents (the contract's glossary/catalog system and CDE-criteria repositories are still unidentified), uses 'system of record' only for the Orchestrator's case-state store, and names no system of record for investment data, whereas the DMBOK2 phrase concerns the authoritative source of the data itself; the ranking of internal over general knowledge has no DMBOK2 counterpart. Proposed wording (for human approval): distinguish 'authoritative source' (an approved document or register an agent may rely on) from 'system of record' (the system holding the authoritative copy of a data domain) in AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md and the Context Agent's content-area list, and keep the internal-over-general ranking as a project rule.

Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Investment Operations Context Agent 'Required distinction': INTERNAL DOCUMENTED POSITION, GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT, INFERENCE, OPEN QUESTION), contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json ('authoritative_sources': a named internal glossary or catalog system, named policy repositories holding CDE criteria, and an exclusion of unstructured email, Teams and chat unless promoted into a named register), AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md ('Authoritative Sources') and schemas/evidence.schema.json (authority_level). The purpose matches Chapter 10: designate which sources count as authoritative, exclude informal ones unless promoted into a named register, and keep claims traceable. The status is Partial because the repository has no counterpart to the chapter's distinction between a system of record and a system of reference, nor to naming a system of record per subject area, and it says 'authoritative source' where the chapter says system of record, system of reference and trusted source. The precedence of internal documented position over general knowledge is a project control the DMBOK2 does not address and should be kept (a candidate for the deviations register). Proposed wording change, for human approval: add a short terminology note that 'authoritative source' in the contracts means an approved evidence source, distinct from a data-level system of record or system of reference, and suggest that future Context and Mapping & Lineage contracts say, for each source platform they name, which of the two it is.

Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (Context Agent: INTERNAL DOCUMENTED POSITION versus GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT), AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md (Authoritative Sources section: approved internal data dictionary, approved mapping specification, approved policy, named repository, approved metadata catalogue) and contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json (authoritative_sources: named glossary/catalog system and named CDE-criteria policy repositories, with email, Teams and chat excluded). The project's 'authoritative source' names where an agent may take evidence from, whereas the DMBOK2's 'authoritative source' and 'system of record' name where a data element's values originate. The words overlap but the senses differ, and none of the files compared designates a system of record for any data element, so the concept is only partly covered; the precedence of internal over industry knowledge is organisational policy, not DMBOK2 guidance. When definitions and lineage artefacts are specified, a system-of-record designation is worth considering as a field.
caveats: The DMBOK2 text read mentions 'system of record' once, in the project-reuse guidance; it does not address which sources an AI assistant may treat as authoritative, so the rule that the internal documented position outranks general knowledge is project-specific.

In the repository 'system of record' appears only in the open question on where Orchestrator case state is held (docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md Open Question 4; docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md), not for investment data.

Whether externally supplied securities and price data counts as an authoritative source is a project decision; the data-as-a-service passage is only an example of such data, not a statement about authority.

The chapter's 'authority' concerns data values and the systems that hold or serve them; the project's 'authoritative sources' are the evidence sources an agent may rely on, plus a rule that INTERNAL DOCUMENTED POSITION outranks GENERAL INDUSTRY CONTEXT. The DMBOK2 does not address that AI-specific precedence rule, which should stay as a project control.

The DMBOK2 does not rank internal documentation above external industry sources; for externally governed reference data it says only that the organisation's reconciled version may differ from the external directory if the differences stay traceable.
The contract states that the glossary or catalog product has not yet been identified, so no concrete system can be designated yet; the gap concerns vocabulary and future designation.
Other units cover reference and master data and integration, where system-of-record guidance may be fuller; this row reflects Chapter 12 usage only.
Where the repository files mention 'system of record' (docs/), it refers to the Orchestrator's case-state store, not to data elements.

positions: The DMBOK2 says data architects create and maintain organisational knowledge about data and the systems it moves through, held in artefacts such as data flow design (which maps data movement to business processes, locations, roles and technical components) and in asset-inventory metadata about systems, and says existing system documentation should be evaluated for accuracy, completeness and level of detail. It also asks that architecture designs be documented as aspirational, implemented or planned for retirement, shows specifications in current, target and transition state, and describes enterprise data or data services offered inside an organisation to functions and operational systems.
rationales: ARCHITECTURE.md lists enterprise data products and relevant source platforms as possible Context Agent content areas (docs/PROPOSED-ARCHITECTURE.md adds source-platform architecture to that agent's scope), which matches the DMBOK2 idea that stewardship needs architectural knowledge of systems and flows. The project does not say which architecture artefacts hold that knowledge, does not say whether a described platform or flow is current, planned or retired (its four evidence labels classify the statement, not the thing described), and leaves data flows to the Mapping & Lineage Agent, so the concept is present but misses elements the DMBOK2 asks for.
caveats: Figures 21 to 26 and Table 6 (context diagram, architecture domains, Zachman framework, enterprise data model layers, subject area models, data flow matrix and diagram) are missing from the converted text; no statement here rests on them.
The Context Agent exists only as a content-area list in ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/PROPOSED-ARCHITECTURE.md and has no contract, so the comparison is against intent, not a built artefact.

'Enterprise data products' is not a DMBOK2 term; the nearest passage describes data services offered inside an organisation, and treating them as equivalent is an interpretation for human confirmation.
proposal_options: Add a three-value state qualifier (current, target, transition) to every Context Agent statement about a source platform or data flow, following the DMBOK2 practice of reflecting architecture specifications in current, target and transition state [DMBOK2-C04-03]; this is a small change to the evidence labels but relies on the organisation's architecture documents saying which state they describe [DMBOK2-C04-14].

Add an eight-value lifecycle status per source platform (Current, Deployment period, Strategic period, Retirement, Preferred, Containment, Emerging, Reviewed), following the DMBOK2 lifecycle projection categories [DMBOK2-C04-15] [DMBOK2-C04-16]; this is finer for platform planning but needs a maintained technology inventory that the project does not have.

positions: DMBOK2 makes classification the starting point of data security: each organisation creates or adopts its own scheme (the text gives a five-level confidentiality scale as an example), Data Stewards decide the level for each data set, and contracts can add their own limits on how information may be used. It also says to keep production data out of non-production environments, that organisations need policies for using data within their risk appetite, and that data security policies must account for data spread across cloud service models; the 2017 text gives no guidance on AI processing, so the service-model passage is only the nearest analogue.
rationales: Compared docs/REPO-CONVENTIONS.md ('No production connectivity': nothing connects to production systems, data or credentials; examples/ and evals/ use synthetic data only) with the open data-handling questions in docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md (open question 3 and the evidence-preservation risk) and docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md (risk 6), and checked schemas/evidence.schema.json, which has no confidentiality or regulatory attribute. The exposure boundary matches DMBOK2 and the policy gap is recorded openly. It is Partial, not Aligned, because the project has no confidentiality or regulatory classification, no statement of who assigns levels, and no permitted-use rule for what may be sent to AI processing or stored in case logs and evidence packs, which DMBOK2 treats as the core of data security. It is not Missing because the boundary rule and the open question both exist. DMBOK2 is general industry context only and internal policy outranks it, so any scheme adopted is provisional until the organisation's own data-handling policy is found.
caveats: Chapters 2 and 7 contain no guidance on generative-AI or LLM processing of organisational data (machine learning appears only in the bias and opacity passages), so the AI-processing half of the concept has no direct DMBOK2 counterpart; the cloud service-model passage is an analogy.

The repo comparison used docs/REPO-CONVENTIONS.md, BUILD-BACKLOG.md, docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md, docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md and schemas/evidence.schema.json, found by keyword search; a classification scheme or data-handling policy may exist elsewhere in the repo or the organisation.
proposal_options: Adopt a confidentiality scale only, taking two or more of the DMBOK2 example levels (DMBOK2-C07-06) as a provisional label, to be replaced by the organisation's own scheme once found (DMBOK2-C07-09), that agents may propose and the Data Steward assigns (DMBOK2-C07-10) and records as metadata (DMBOK2-C07-16); the cost is one optional field named differently from the capability 'classification' already used in schemas/agent-contract.schema.json, plus labelling rules, with schema, contract and test changes made together.

Adopt the DMBOK2 risk classification of critical, high and moderate risk data (DMBOK2-C07-03) as the label instead of confidentiality levels; the cost is the same single field plus class definitions the organisation would have to write for its own Investment Operations content.

Adopt two separate labels, a confidentiality level plus regulatory categories (DMBOK2-C07-05 and DMBOK2-C07-06), because DMBOK2 treats confidentiality and regulation as distinct drivers of restriction; the cost is two fields and a category list that must be written and kept current.

positions: DMBOK2 counts truthfulness and transparency about the sources, uses and intent of data handling as part of ethical handling, says that leaving out required context lets a presentation imply meaning the data does not support, and notes that the logic and lineage of predictive algorithms become hard to track as they grow more complex. It expects ethics to be set out in policy and a code of ethics backed by training and oversight, and says automated monitoring alone is not enough because people must reflect on possible bias.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md (Important non-goals 'hides uncertainty' and 'presents inferred organisational policy as fact'; Evidence policy; Confidence policy), README.md (purpose line favouring 'trustworthy, auditable, explainable stewardship'; principle 4), schemas/agent-contract.schema.json (fixed confidence_labels) and schemas/evidence.schema.json (authority_level separates authoritative_internal, general_industry and inferred). The core matches DMBOK2: both treat misleading by omission as unethical, the project turns the duty into mandatory labels, and its Data Steward evaluation step agrees with the DMBOK2 view that automated checks alone are not enough. It is Partial rather than Aligned because the project states this only as a rule for AI output, in its own terms (uncertainty, inference, confidence) rather than DMBOK2's truthfulness and transparency, and nothing in the files read says where the wider elements DMBOK2 treats as essential sit: an ethics policy or code with training and oversight, and attention to bias in analysis. Those are mostly organisation-level, so the gap is one of wording and scoping, not new structure.
caveats: The opacity passage (DMBOK2-C02-07) is an end-note about predictive algorithms in the 2017 text; it is the nearest statement to AI transparency in Chapters 2 and 7 and is not guidance on generative AI.

The people-impact, privacy-law and ethical-principles material in Chapter 2 concerns analytics on personal data and was not mapped to repo artefacts; the gap noted here is about wording and scope, not evidence that the project mishandles personal data.

positions: DMBOK2 expects regulatory compliance to be demonstrable: data requirements and controls must be measurable and auditable, controls need an audit trail because without one there is no evidence of compliance, and a central inventory should link each regulation to the data subject areas it affects and to the policies written to comply, with the regulatory classification serving as the foundation for answering audits. It also observes that the logic and lineage of learning-machine decisions become harder to follow as models grow more complex.
rationales: Compared ARCHITECTURE.md (the Investment Operations Context Agent lists 'regulatory reporting' as a content area and must distinguish internal documented position, general industry context, inference and open question), README.md (purpose line 'trustworthy, auditable, explainable stewardship'; principle 5, every material conclusion traceable to evidence) and schemas/evidence.schema.json (each evidence item carries source_id, location, authority_level, direct_or_inferred and timestamp). Claim-level traceability matches DMBOK2's demand for auditable evidence of compliance and is more demanding for AI conclusions. It is Partial because the traceability is defined for AI claims rather than as an audit trail over stored case evidence, whose retention and access rules docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md and docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md record as an open question; because the repo has no inventory of the regulations that bind the data in scope (outside the DMBOK review materials, that one ARCHITECTURE.md bullet is the only place the word 'regulatory' or 'regulation' appears); and because 'regulatory reporting' is a business topic whereas DMBOK2's regulatory compliance concerns legal limits on handling data. The inventory is an organisation-level artefact, so the repo change is wording that states which sense of 'regulatory' is meant and names the organisation's regulation inventory and case audit trail as items still to be located or defined.
caveats: The sample regulation inventory (Table 13) is an image missing from the conversion; its layout is unverifiable from text and was not relied on.

DMBOK2 audit and compliance guidance addresses controls operated by people over data systems; applying it to AI-generated conclusions is an analogy, and the opacity end-note (DMBOK2-C02-07) predates generative AI.

positions: The DMBOK2 defines an operating model as a framework of roles, responsibilities and decision-making processes rather than an org chart, describes decentralized, network, centralized, hybrid and federated patterns, and says no structure is perfect and most organisations begin decentralized. Stewards may sit at enterprise, business-unit or functional level; the network pattern adds a RACI matrix and the hybrid pattern pairs a central Center of Excellence with business-unit groups.
rationales: Compared docs/PROPOSED-ARCHITECTURE.md (Layer 2, the Operational Stewardship Team, with the human Data Steward at both ends of the flow and a human governance sign-off for Layer 1) and README.md (Operational Stewardship Team). They describe AI agents working under one human Data Steward, with decision rights set by the 'AI proposes, evidence supports, the Data Steward evaluates, the appropriate human owner approves' principle and an unnamed governance owner. That documents decision rights for the agents, but no human operating model in DMBOK2 terms is given: no chosen pattern, accountability map, committee or forum, or statement of the steward's organisational level. If the owner prefers to keep the single-steward structure without adopting a DMBOK2 pattern, a record-deviation is the alternative to the options below, which are proposals only.
caveats: The Agent Factory and the Operational Stewardship Team are AI-system constructs with no DMBOK2 counterpart; only the human operating model is compared here.
Business-versus-technical steward types are not defined in Chapters 15-16 (Chapter 16 groups roles as business, IT and hybrid); the steward-type taxonomy lies in a chapter outside this range.
Operating-model diagrams (Figures 106-111) are missing from the conversion; this row uses the prose descriptions only, and the diagrams themselves are unverifiable from text.
proposal_options: Option A - decentralized, functional-level steward (the current de facto position): record that the Investment Operations Data Steward works at functional level in a decentralized model and name the forum used for collaboration; the DMBOK2 notes most organisations start here but that data ownership is harder to define. Backed by DMBOK2-C16-12, DMBOK2-C16-33 and DMBOK2-C16-07.

Option B - network model: keep the single steward and add a RACI matrix linking the steward, Data Owners, SMEs, operations teams and the governance owner, which the DMBOK2 says adds accountability without changing organisation charts. Backed by DMBOK2-C16-08 and DMBOK2-C16-09.
Option C - hybrid model: pair the business-unit steward with a central Center of Excellence and an executive steering committee, as in the DMBOK2 hybrid pattern. Backed by DMBOK2-C16-11.

positions: Chapter 15 describes a maturity assessment as rating data management capability against a framework of five or six levels using evidence-supported criteria (grouped, for example, by activity, tools, standards, and people and resources), scoped if needed to one knowledge area, run against a baseline and repeated on a published schedule, and it ties the practice to the governance function. It names published frameworks such as CMMI-DMM and the financial-services DCAM and says the DMBOK2 itself can serve as a checklist for such an assessment.
rationales: Compared HANDOFF.md ('Success criteria'): ten qualitative conditions for a governed, traceable capability (for example 'agents know their boundaries', 'claims are traceable') with no scale, baseline, evidence-rating method or review cadence; no maturity measure exists anywhere in the repository. The criteria work as a target-state description, which is one element of the DMBOK2 assessment cycle, but not as an assessment of capability against levels and criteria. If the owner decides a maturity measure is out of scope for this project, a record-deviation can replace the options below, which are proposals only; the DMBOK2 is general industry context and internal policy outranks it.
caveats: Figures 103-105 (context diagram, example maturity model, example visualisation) and Table 33 (risks and mitigations for an assessment) are not available in the conversion; their content is unverifiable from text and was not used.
The DMBOK2 says a baseline understanding and some organisational maturity are needed before an assessment can be run, so readiness for this project was not assumed.
The ten Success criteria also include AI-specific conditions (agents can be evaluated independently, governance can be applied to the agents themselves) on which the DMBOK2 is silent.
proposal_options: Option A - scoped assessment with a published framework: choose a published data management maturity framework (the DMBOK2 names CMMI-DMM, the financial-services DCAM and others), evaluate several before choosing, and limit the first assessment to Investment Operations data stewardship; the DMBOK2 cautions that a baseline understanding and some organisational maturity are needed first. additional_content.topic: Bias in analysis: hunch and search
additional_content.why_relevant: The Exception and Root-Cause agent synthesises hypotheses from a curated evidence packet, and DMBOK2 names using only the data that confirms a hunch as an analysis bias that the Data Steward's evaluation should look for.

additional_content.topic: Least privilege applies to processes and programs
additional_content.why_relevant: DMBOK2 applies least privilege to processes and programs as well as people, which is the nearest industry hook for the permitted-tool and minimum-permission limits in the agent contracts.

additional_content.topic: Confidential data proliferation
additional_content.why_relevant: The project's own risk notes say case logs and stewardship packs will hold copies of sensitive Investment Operations content, and DMBOK2 frames the number of copies of confidential data as a measurable breach risk.

additional_content.topic: Data Stewards work with Information Security and Corporate Counsel
additional_content.why_relevant: It names the functions a Data Steward coordinates with on policy compliance, which may help identify the currently unnamed human owner for classification and regulatory questions.

additional_content.topic: Independence of auditors
additional_content.why_relevant: DMBOK2 requires auditors to be independent of the data or process they audit, which matches the project's concern that the producer of a conclusion must not also certify it.

additional_content.topic: Sensitivity classification belongs in the data definition process
additional_content.why_relevant: It places sensitivity classification inside the step where data is defined, which bears on the Definition and CDE agent and on any definition template.

additional_content.topic: Issue management: logging, tracking and documenting resolutions
additional_content.why_relevant: Exception and root-cause work and any escalation need an issue record with assigned actions and documented resolutions, a control set the DMBOK2 describes in section 2.10 and that no assigned concept covers.

additional_content.topic: Regulatory compliance as a governance driver and duty
additional_content.why_relevant: Investment Operations is a regulated financial-services setting, and the project files compared do not name regulatory compliance as a driver of stewardship work.

additional_content.topic: Data quality evaluation dimensions in a sample certified-data policy
additional_content.why_relevant: The sample names accuracy, completeness, consistency, accessibility, uniqueness, compliance and efficiency, which bears on the Data-Quality-Dimension taxonomy that Phase 0b of docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md requires, though it is only an illustration.

additional_content.topic: Governance control points embedded in the development lifecycle
additional_content.why_relevant: The Agent Factory's staged review gates are lifecycle control points of the kind the DMBOK2 asks governance to build into system and application development.

additional_content.topic: Governance as an ongoing, principle-based programme
additional_content.why_relevant: README.md's ten design principles could be cross-referenced to the DMBOK2 view that governance is ongoing and that policy rests on stated guiding principles.

additional_content.topic: Readiness assessment before building governance capability
additional_content.why_relevant: A baseline assessment of capability, maturity and effectiveness underpins both planning and later measurement, which bears on the Phase 0 and 0b sequencing and on the metrics proposed under A-06.

additional_content.topic: Business rules harvesting and the four rule categories
additional_content.why_relevant: The DMBOK2 names data stewards among those who extract business rules from documentation and code and gives a four-way rule taxonomy, which bears on the evidence used by the Definition & CDE and Data Quality agents.

additional_content.topic: Profiling to test assumptions against actual data, balanced with privacy
additional_content.why_relevant: It supports the project rule that unsupported assumptions must be flagged and bears on the Mapping & Lineage Agent's open risk of reading production data values.

additional_content.topic: Process controls for data movement
additional_content.why_relevant: The DMBOK2 treats accuracy and completeness controls on data movement as part of integration design, which is where the evidence for an Exception & Root-Cause Agent about failed loads would originate.

additional_content.topic: Pairing a Data Steward with a data architect for each subject area
additional_content.why_relevant: It bears on the project's single-steward operating model, since the DMBOK2 pairs a steward with an architect at subject-area and entity level.

additional_content.topic: Interface sprawl, data copies and replication as sources of inconsistency
additional_content.why_relevant: It names concrete structural causes of inconsistent data that an Exception & Root-Cause Agent could test as hypotheses.

additional_content.topic: Event-triggered governance reviews and approval controls for integration changes
additional_content.why_relevant: It shows one way to map escalation triggers to governance reviews and approval gates, relevant to the project's escalation conditions and human-approval points.

additional_content.topic: Monitoring shared-data movement for lineage, root-cause analysis and latency
additional_content.why_relevant: Section 4.2 lists lineage identification and root-cause support among the reasons to monitor how shared data flows, which bears on the Mapping & Lineage and Exception & Root-Cause agents.

additional_content.topic: Controlled, approved and communicated change to Reference Data values
additional_content.why_relevant: It parallels the project's human-approval gate for production changes and could inform how change approvals are recorded.

additional_content.topic: Reference Data set metadata (steward, source, update schedule, consuming processes)
additional_content.why_relevant: The listed attributes are a candidate checklist for the project's metadata and data dictionary artefacts, although Table 23 that illustrates them is a missing figure.

additional_content.topic: Data sharing agreements and service levels for shared data
additional_content.why_relevant: Agreements that state what data is shared and on what conditions, backed by service levels and metrics in the same section, relate to the project's data contract and upstream dependency responsibilities.

additional_content.topic: Governance metrics for Reference and Master Data
additional_content.why_relevant: Section 6.1 lists quality, change-activity, service-level and steward-coverage metrics that could seed the project's governance reporting.

additional_content.topic: Computational and industry Reference Data such as exchange-rate tables
additional_content.why_relevant: Managed exchange-rate style data is the kind of shared reference data that valuation and NAV depend on, which the Context agent lists as content areas (our inference, not a DMBOK2 statement).

additional_content.topic: Operational metadata as evidence for exception and root-cause work
additional_content.why_relevant: Operational metadata, which the chapter says covers details of processing and accessing data, includes audit, balance and control results that the Data Quality and Exception & Root-Cause agents could use as evidence.

additional_content.topic: Definition-writing guidelines and templates
additional_content.why_relevant: The chapter gives concrete drafting checks (no circular definitions, completeness statements) and names an ISO formulation standard for data definitions, which could back the checks applied to candidate definitions.

additional_content.topic: Metadata quality metrics and coverage
additional_content.why_relevant: Repository completeness and the percentage of attributes with definitions are suggested measures that could ground governance reporting and the missing-definition findings.

additional_content.topic: Sensitivity of metadata itself
additional_content.why_relevant: Some metadata would reveal the existence of highly protected data, which bears on what agents with read access to glossary and catalog content may surface in their outputs.

additional_content.topic: Consumer feedback route for incorrect or out-of-date metadata
additional_content.why_relevant: A defined feedback mechanism fits the continuous-improvement scope and gives stewards a way to learn of stale definitions.

additional_content.topic: Risk of SME knowledge loss
additional_content.why_relevant: The chapter names dependence on a few subject-matter experts as a metadata risk, matching the project's need to flag questions that require SME or Data Owner input.

additional_content.topic: Manually-directed correction and the risk of direct production fixes
additional_content.why_relevant: DMBOK2's pattern of tool-proposed corrections that the data steward reviews and approves, and its warning against committing fixes directly in production, parallel the project's propose-then-approve principle and its non-goal of changing production data.

additional_content.topic: Data profiling output as assessed evidence, not conclusion
additional_content.why_relevant: Profiling results would feed the Data Quality and Exception agents as evidence, and DMBOK2 says they need analyst assessment and do not by themselves identify root causes or business impact.

additional_content.topic: Plan-do-check-act improvement cycle
additional_content.why_relevant: Offers an industry lifecycle for the continuous-improvement responsibility listed in README.md.

additional_content.topic: Statistical process control
additional_content.why_relevant: Control limits and the split between common and special causes could give a statistical basis for spotting recurring exception patterns and informing, but not setting, human-approved thresholds.

additional_content.topic: Data quality measurement results held in a Metadata repository
additional_content.why_relevant: Supports the 'Stewardship as Code' idea in ARCHITECTURE.md of keeping quality rules, exceptions and evidence in shared, version-controlled stores.

additional_content.topic: Prioritising issues by business impact and cost
additional_content.why_relevant: Gives factors a steward could use to rank recurring exception clusters before routing them for human decision.

additional_content.topic: Guiding principles as the basis for decisions
additional_content.why_relevant: The project's ten design principles and its 'AI proposes' authority model play the role the DMBOK2 gives to guiding principles that make decisions consistent.

additional_content.topic: Evidence-supported consensus on current state
additional_content.why_relevant: Rating current-state capability from proof of practice mirrors the project's rule that every material conclusion is traceable to evidence.

additional_content.topic: Training stewards, owners and custodians, including on new tools
additional_content.why_relevant: The humans who evaluate and approve AI proposals will need focused training, and a search of the main project documents found no training or onboarding plan.

additional_content.topic: Critical success factors for a Data Management Organization
additional_content.why_relevant: Executive sponsorship, clear vision, change management and leadership alignment give the owner a ready checklist for sustaining the capability once it is built.

additional_content.topic: Phased introduction through pilots and waves
additional_content.why_relevant: Piloting in waves matches the project's incremental build sequence and could frame how the capability is rolled out beyond a first pilot.

additional_content.topic: Aligning the data quality group with the data management operating model
additional_content.why_relevant: The Data Quality Agent's outputs will meet an organisation's data quality group, whose operating model the DMBOK2 says should align with the wider data management organisation.
